timeline.title: Born near Vinci
timeline.text: Leonardo was born on 15 April 1452 in or near the Tuscan village of Vinci, possibly at Anchiano. His parents were not married: his father was the notary Piero da Vinci and his mother was Caterina di Meo Lippi. As a boy he had only a basic, informal education in reading, writing and arithmetic.

timeline.title: Into Verrocchio's workshop
timeline.text: His family moved to Florence in the mid-1460s. At about 14 he joined the busy workshop of the artist Andrea del Verrocchio as a studio boy, and by 17 he was an apprentice. There he learned his craft by doing, alongside other young artists.

timeline.title: A master painter
timeline.text: At about 20 he qualified as a master in the Guild of Saint Luke, the guild of artists in Florence. He still stayed and worked with Verrocchio.

timeline.title: The Arno valley drawing
timeline.text: His earliest known dated work is a pen-and-ink drawing of the Arno valley from 1473. It shows his eye for landscape and the natural world.

timeline.title: The angel and the Annunciation
timeline.text: Around 1472 to 1475 he painted a young angel in Verrocchio's Baptism of Christ. In the same years he painted the Annunciation. Both are now in the Uffizi in Florence.

timeline.title: His own commissions
timeline.text: In January 1478 he received an independent commission for an altarpiece in the Palazzo della Signoria. Around 1474 to 1478 he also painted the portrait of Ginevra de' Benci.

timeline.title: The unfinished Adoration
timeline.text: The monks of San Donato in Scopeto asked him to paint the Adoration of the Magi. He left for Milan the next year with only the underdrawing done. The monks gave the job to another painter. Leaving work unfinished became a pattern in his life.

timeline.title: A letter to the Duke of Milan
timeline.text: Lorenzo de' Medici sent him to Ludovico Sforza, ruler of Milan. Leonardo wrote to Ludovico offering his skills mainly as an engineer and designer of weapons, and also as a painter. He moved to Milan and worked there until 1499.

timeline.title: The Virgin of the Rocks
timeline.text: In April 1483 Leonardo and the de Predis brothers signed a contract to paint an altarpiece for a chapel in San Francesco Grande, Milan. The first version is now in the Louvre. According to the National Gallery, he sold it because he was not paid enough and later painted a second version, now in London.

timeline.title: Lady with an Ermine
timeline.text: Around 1489 to 1491 he painted Cecilia Gallerani of Ludovico's court holding a small white animal. The portrait is now one of Poland's national treasures, in the Czartoryski Museum in Kraków.

timeline.title: The Vitruvian Man
timeline.text: Around 1490 he drew a man inside a circle and a square, testing the ancient Roman architect Vitruvius's ideas about body proportions against his own measurements. That year he was also consulted on the building of Pavia Cathedral.

timeline.title: The horse that was never cast
timeline.text: For years he worked on a giant bronze horse for the Sforza family and made a full model. In November 1494 Ludovico gave the bronze set aside for it to be made into a cannon for war instead. The horse was never cast.

timeline.title: The Last Supper
timeline.text: Around 1495 to 1498 he painted the Last Supper on the dining hall wall of the convent of Santa Maria delle Grazie. He used an experimental method, tempera on a dry wall instead of fresco, so he could work slowly and revise. The paint began to flake soon after he finished.

timeline.title: Leaving Milan
timeline.text: After the French overthrew Ludovico, Leonardo left Milan with his assistant Salai and the mathematician Luca Pacioli. In Venice he worked as a military architect and engineer before going back to Florence.

timeline.title: Engineer for Cesare Borgia
timeline.text: In 1502 he served the military leader Cesare Borgia as an engineer, travelling through central Italy. For him he drew a map of the town of Imola.

timeline.title: The Mona Lisa begins
timeline.text: Back in Florence, he rejoined the painters' guild on 18 October 1503 and began a portrait of Lisa del Giocondo, a silk merchant's wife. He kept working on it for years. Scholars disagree on how long: some place much of the work after 1513.

timeline.title: The battle wall
timeline.text: He spent about two years on a huge mural of the Battle of Anghiari for the city's council hall, but never finished it. In January 1504 he sat on the committee that chose where to place Michelangelo's David. His father died that year.

timeline.title: Notes on the flight of birds
timeline.text: Around 1505 he filled a small notebook of 18 sheets with studies of how birds fly and designs for flying machines. He noticed that a bird's centre of gravity is not the same as its centre of pressure.

timeline.title: Back to Milan, and a pupil
timeline.text: The French governor Charles d'Amboise called him back to Milan. A young nobleman, Francesco Melzi, became his pupil and, years later, his heir.

timeline.title: Water, fossils and moonlight
timeline.text: Around 1506 to 1508, and again around 1510 to 1512, he wrote the notes now called the Codex Leicester. They study how water moves, why sea fossils are found on mountains, and why the dark part of the Moon glows faintly, which he explained as light reflected from the Earth.

timeline.title: Studying the human body
timeline.text: In 1510 and 1511 he worked with Marcantonio della Torre, professor of anatomy at the University of Pavia. He made more than 240 detailed anatomical drawings and planned a book on anatomy that was never published.

timeline.title: Rome
timeline.text: When a Medici became Pope Leo X, Leonardo went to Rome in September 1513. He lived in the Belvedere of the Vatican palace until 1516.

timeline.title: Invited to France
timeline.text: King Francis I of France invited him into his service. Leonardo moved to France in 1516 and was given the manor house of Clos Luce, near the royal castle at Amboise.

timeline.title: A paralysed right hand
timeline.text: Around 1517, when he was 65, it was recorded that his right hand was paralysed. Leonardo was left-handed and wrote mostly in mirror writing, from right to left.

timeline.title: The Mona Lisa goes to the king
timeline.text: The Louvre says Francis I bought the Mona Lisa from Leonardo in 1518. Other records disagree: his assistant Salai owned a "Gioconda" when he died in 1524, and some scholars think the king got the painting only after Leonardo's death.

timeline.title: Death at Clos Luce
timeline.text: Leonardo died at Clos Luce on 2 May 1519, aged 67, possibly of a stroke. He was buried at Amboise. Francesco Melzi was his main heir and received his drawings, tools and books.

timeline.title: The notebooks scatter
timeline.text: Melzi kept the notebooks safe until his death in 1570. His son took little interest, and pages were given away and sold. The sculptor Pompeo Leoni later cut up and rebound many sheets into the Codex Atlanticus. Today about 13,000 pages survive in collections across Europe.

timeline.title: The notebooks in English
timeline.text: Jean Paul Richter published a large selection of the notebooks with English translations in 1888. It is now free on Project Gutenberg.

timeline.title: The Mona Lisa stolen
timeline.text: A Louvre worker, Vincenzo Peruggia, stole the Mona Lisa on 21 August 1911. He was caught trying to sell it in Florence, and it went back to the Louvre in January 1914.

timeline.title: The Last Supper restored
timeline.text: After surviving a 1943 bombing of the convent, the Last Supper went through a long restoration that began in 1978. It went back on view on 28 May 1999.

works.title: The Baptism of Christ (the angel)
works.text: Painted with his teacher Verrocchio around 1472 to 1475; Leonardo painted the young angel. Held by the Uffizi Gallery, Florence.

works.title: Annunciation
works.text: An early painting of about 1472 to 1476. Held by the Uffizi Gallery, Florence.

works.title: Ginevra de' Benci
works.text: A portrait of a young Florentine woman, about 1474 to 1478. Held by the National Gallery of Art, Washington, D.C., since 1967; the only Leonardo painting on public view in the Americas.

works.title: Adoration of the Magi (unfinished)
works.text: Left as an underdrawing when he moved to Milan. Held by the Uffizi Gallery, Florence, since 1670.

works.title: The Virgin of the Rocks
works.text: Two versions of one altarpiece: the first in the Musée du Louvre, Paris, and the second, finished 1506 to 1508, in the National Gallery, London.

works.title: Lady with an Ermine
works.text: A portrait of Cecilia Gallerani in oil on walnut, about 1489 to 1491. Held by the Czartoryski Museum, part of the National Museum in Kraków, Poland.

works.title: Vitruvian Man
works.text: A study of human proportions in pen, ink and watercolour. Held by the Gallerie dell'Accademia, Venice.

works.title: The Sforza Horse (never cast)
works.text: A giant bronze horse for the rulers of Milan. He made the model, but the metal went to make a cannon.

works.title: The Last Supper
works.text: A wall painting of about 1495 to 1498, still in place in the refectory of Santa Maria delle Grazie, Milan.

works.title: Map of Imola
works.text: A town plan drawn for Cesare Borgia while Leonardo worked as his engineer.

works.title: Mona Lisa
works.text: Portrait of Lisa del Giocondo, begun in 1503 and worked on for years. Held by the Musée du Louvre, Paris.

works.title: The Battle of Anghiari (lost)
works.text: A huge battle mural for Florence's council hall, left unfinished and now lost.

works.title: Codex on the Flight of Birds
works.text: An 18-sheet notebook on bird flight and flying machines. Held by the Royal Library, Turin.

works.title: Saint John the Baptist
works.text: A late painting of about 1507 to 1516. Held by the Musée du Louvre, Paris.

works.title: Codex Leicester
works.text: 72 pages on water, fossils and the light of the Moon. The only major Leonardo notebook in private hands; owned by a private collector since 1994.

works.title: Anatomical drawings
works.text: More than 240 detailed drawings of the human body, many made with Marcantonio della Torre. Many are in the Royal Library at Windsor Castle.

works.title: Codex Atlanticus
works.text: 1,119 sheets from 1478 to 1519 on flight, weapons, machines, mathematics and more, gathered into 12 volumes after his death. Held by the Biblioteca Ambrosiana, Milan.
